planting.note: Divide and transplant container-grown crowns in spring once soil has warmed, before new fiddleheads unfurl.

directions: One of the most finely dissected of the historic Divisilobum group of Victorian soft shield fern sports, forming a dense, congested, almost moss-like mound of lacy, multiply-divided evergreen fronds. This AGM selection is more compact and tightly textured than plain Divisilobum, making it a refined specimen for a shaded rock garden or container. Grows best in humus-rich, well-drained soil with reliable moisture and dappled to full shade. Divide established clumps in spring to propagate true to type.

planting.note: Divide and transplant crowns in early spring as the bright golden-brown fiddleheads begin to uncurl.

directions: An AGM-winning crested selection of the golden-scaled male fern, distinct from the taller 'Cristata The King' and narrower 'Cristata Angustata' clones, with broad, semi-evergreen fronds terminating in neat, fan-like crests. Fiddleheads emerge covered in warm golden-brown scales in early spring, a signature trait of the affinis group. Tolerates dry shade once established better than most woodland ferns, making it useful under mature trees.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in spring into humus-rich woodland soil; establishes readily in deep shade.

directions: A long-cultivated AGM Victorian sport of the common male fern in which each pinna and the frond apex terminate in a neat crest, giving an otherwise robust, coarse-textured woodland fern a more refined, tasseled silhouette. Vigorous and tolerant of a wide range of soils, including heavier clay, and reliably hardy. One of the easiest crested ferns for a beginner shade gardener to establish.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring; give room for the heavily branched frond tips to display without crowding.

directions: An AGM-listed, heavily tasseled selection of the male fern named for the Victorian fern-hunter who found it, bearing dense, congested, multi-branched crests at both the frond tip and along each pinna, more exaggerated than the plainer 'Grandiceps' clone. The overall effect is a distinctly architectural, almost coral-like frond silhouette. Easy and hardy, it suits a shaded border where its unusual texture can be appreciated at close range.

planting.note: Divide creeping rhizomes in autumn as new winter growth begins, matching this fern's summer-dormant cycle.

directions: An AGM crested form within the Welsh polypody's Cristatum Group, bearing densely congested, repeatedly branched crests at the tip of each frond, held low over creeping, felted rhizomes. Like the species, it is winter-green and summer-dormant, dying back in dry heat and flushing new fronds with autumn rains. Best grown over a shaded rock ledge, low wall, or tree-trunk niche where its rhizomes can creep across the surface.

planting.note: Transplant divisions into alkaline, humus-rich soil in spring; tolerates lime and limestone crevices well.

directions: An AGM-winning narrow-fronded form of the hart's tongue fern, with glossy, leathery, undivided strap-shaped fronds noticeably slimmer than the species type, giving a more upright, grass-like clump. Evergreen and architectural, it associates well with hostas and hellebores in deep shade and tolerates limy or alkaline soils better than most ferns. A classic Victorian fern-collecting selection still offered by specialist nurseries.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in spring into light, humus-rich soil; this sterile hybrid is propagated only by division.

directions: A sterile Victorian-era hybrid maidenhair, raised by Thomas Moore from southern maidenhair (Adiantum capillus-veneris) crossed with a finer tropical relative, combining delicate, finely divided bright green pinnae on wiry black stipes with noticeably greater cold tolerance than either parent. This AGM selection remains evergreen in mild winters but dies back and resprouts reliably from the rhizome after harder frosts. Grow in organic, moisture-retentive soil in part shade, sheltered from drying wind.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring once frost danger has passed, in constantly moist, humus-rich shade.

directions: A large, leathery-fronded hard fern from the cool temperate rainforests of Chile and Patagonia, known locally as costilla de vaca ("cow's rib") for the strongly ribbed, once-pinnate fronds held in an upright shuttlecock crown. With age it slowly builds a short, stout, fibrous trunk reminiscent of a true tree fern. Needs constant moisture, rich organic soil, and deep shade; established plants tolerate brief cold spells but benefit from mulch or trunk wrapping in marginal zones.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in spring into reliably moist, acidic woodland soil in deep shade.

directions: An AGM-winning crested form of the broad buckler fern, with conspicuously scaly stipes and broadly triangular, dark green fronds that terminate in congested, multi-branched crests at the tip and on each pinna. Forms a dense, architectural clump that prefers consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in heavy shade, making it well suited to a damp woodland floor or streamside planting where plainer buckler ferns might scorch.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container specimens in spring in constantly moist, rich soil along a shaded bank or streamside.

directions: A large, cycad-like evergreen hard fern native to afromontane forest margins and riverbanks from South Africa north to Uganda and Nigeria, distinguished from similar tree-like Blechnum by its unevenly based pinnae. Mature plants slowly develop a short, stout, trunk-like base topped by a crown of long, once-pinnate fronds. Thrives in constantly moist, shaded woodland conditions and makes a striking specimen where winters stay mild.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown divisions in spring into warm, humid, humus-rich shade once nights stay above 55 degrees F.

directions: A distinctive maidenhair fern from Mexico, the Caribbean, and northern South America that breaks from the typical dissected maidenhair look: its broad pinnae are simple and undivided rather than finely cut, with a leathery texture. New fronds emerge coppery-pink before maturing to deep glossy green. Needs warmth, high humidity, and constant moisture, making it best suited to a frost-free shaded garden, greenhouse, or terrarium rather than open ground in temperate climates.
